title: The dart of grief
hook: life is short and uncertain; draw out the dart of lamentation

segments.voice: Yesterday: well spoken, four marks of good speech, and a poet who put them in verse. Your line: true and kind. Today, the hardest goodbye of all.

There's a drawer in many homes that nobody opens much. A watch that stopped. A card in a handwriting you'd know anywhere. A phone number you can't quite bring yourself to delete. Grief has a way of lodging somewhere and staying. The Salla Sutta, the discourse on the dart, eighth in the Sutta Nipata's third chapter, doesn't open with comfort. It opens with the plain facts of death, and then a picture every archer and every healer in ancient India would have known: something sharp, stuck in the chest, that has to come out.
screen: `A DRAWER NOBODY OPENS.` → `GRIEF LODGES AND STAYS.` → `THE SALLA SUTTA, SN 3.8.`

segments.voice: The verses begin bluntly. The life of mortals is unmarked by any sign of how long it will last, short, and tied up with pain. There's no way for those born not to die. Then the images pile up. As ripe fruit is in danger of falling early, so the born are always in danger of death. As clay pots made by a potter all end up broken, so it is with life. Young and old, foolish and wise, all go under death's power. Even as relatives look on, weeping, each one is led away. Then the turn. The wise, seeing how the world is, don't add grief on grief. Weeping and wailing, the poem says, don't bring back the one who's gone; they only harm the one who weeps, who grows thin and pale, while the dead are not helped at all. So draw out the dart: the dart of lamenting, of longing, of grief, and you'll find peace. Two things are worth noticing. First, the dart is in the mourner, not in the one who died. The poem isn't saying the loss doesn't matter. It's saying the wound is real and can heal. Second, Pali salla is a barbed arrow or a splinter, the thing a healer pulls out. The poem is firm: lamenting helps no one. But its picture is a healer's, not a judge's. A barb is drawn out with care, not something you're blamed for carrying.
screen: `NO SIGN OF HOW LONG.` · `RIPE FRUIT, CLAY POTS.` · `WEEPING DOESN'T BRING THEM BACK.` · `THE DART IS IN THE MOURNER.` · then, large: `DRAW OUT THE DART.`

segments.voice: If there's someone you've lost, a person, an animal, a time of your life, let them come to mind, and find where the feeling sits: the chest, the throat, behind the eyes. Breathe near it, the way you'd sit beside someone in a hospital bed. If nothing comes, think of someone who is grieving, and simply wish them ease.
Salla, a barbed dart. In the Salla Sutta, lamenting lodged in the one who mourns, a real wound, which can be drawn out.
Your line: draw out the dart. Gently, the way a healer would. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Verses on impermanence are often chanted at Buddhist funerals and memorial services, and in many Theravada communities monks are invited to chant and teach for the family in the days after a death.

original.note: Pali salla: a dart, barbed arrow or splinter. the Salla Sutta is Sn 3.8.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism says don't grieve.
what it means: the dart is real and it's in the mourner; the poem asks that it be drawn out, not denied.
what a scholar hears: salla, the barbed arrow, recurs in the early texts: the arrow of craving, the poisoned arrow of MN 63, the second arrow of SN 36.6.

chat.says: My grandmother died last month. Does Buddhism say I shouldn't grieve?
options: The poem calls grief a dart in the mourner: a real wound that can heal.
Yes; the poem says grief is a fault you should be ashamed of.
It says the loss doesn't matter, since everyone dies anyway.
chat.meaning: The Salla Sutta says the dart is lodged in the one who mourns: the wound is real, and like a barb, it can be drawn out with care.

notes: Sn 3.8 paraphrased throughout. Confirm the ripe-fruit and potter's-pot similes, the relatives looking on, and 'grows thin and pale'.
The listener is invited to grieve gently; the script avoids telling anyone to stop mourning. A Keeper may want to add how communities actually support mourners.
Earlier days touch arrows: day 74 (Kisa Gotami), 257 (the second arrow), 346 (the poisoned arrow). Today's angle is the dart lodged in the mourner.
